title: One input: does budget tightening predict productivity growth?
plain: Drew the best straight line from the size of a budget tightening (ΔCAPB) to TFP growth over the following two years, then tested it on countries the model had never seen.
lesson: The effect is real (negative and statistically significant), but as a predictor it is barely better than guessing the average. Significant is not the same as predictive.

title: Several inputs at once
plain: Added the four thesis controls and a yes/no consolidation flag, scaled the inputs using the training countries only, and trained with vectorized gradient descent. Repeated the unseen-country test and tried adding ΔCAPB².
lesson: The effect estimate moved close to the thesis, but prediction did not improve: a gain of about 9 % on one set of hidden countries turns into a loss when every country takes a turn. One test can flatter a model. Looking closely at the inputs also exposed and fixed a real error in two thesis controls.

title: A yes/no question: which consolidations are followed by weak growth?
plain: Switched from predicting a number to a yes/no answer: is a consolidation followed by below-median TFP growth? Used logistic regression with my own gradient descent, tried several regularization strengths (λ), and repeated the unseen-country tests. Then repeated everything with each episode compared with other countries in the same year.
lesson: The first model to beat the simple guess in the fairer test, but only slightly. Most of that came from timing: once each episode is compared with its own year, the model wins in only 13 of 24 countries and in about half of random splits. A model can predict for the wrong reason.
